items.title: Article 368 — The Amendment Procedure
items.body:
## Power to amend

- **Article 368** in **Part XX** gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal. The procedure was **borrowed from the South African Constitution**.
- An amendment bill can be introduced **only in either House of Parliament**, never in a State Legislature, and does **not** require prior permission of the President.
- Since the **24th Amendment (1971)**, the President **must** give assent and can neither withhold nor return the bill.

## Three ways to amend

| Route | Requirement | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple majority** (outside Art 368) | 50% of members present and voting | New states, citizenship, quorum, salaries |
| **Special majority** | Majority of total membership **+** 2/3 of members present and voting | Fundamental Rights, DPSP |
| **Special majority + state ratification** | Above **+** approval by ≥half the states (simple majority) | Federal provisions — President's election, Seventh Schedule, distribution of powers |

- Only the last two are amendments **within the scope of Article 368**; simple-majority changes are technically not counted as constitutional amendments.
keyPoints: Article 368 (Part XX) governs amendments; procedure borrowed from South Africa.
Amendment bill can be introduced only in Parliament, not in State Legislatures.
24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent to an amendment bill mandatory.
Special majority = majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting.
Federal provisions additionally need ratification by at least half the state legislatures.
Simple-majority changes (new states, citizenship) fall outside the scope of Article 368.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Amendments of the Indian Constitution

items.title: Landmark Constitutional Amendments
items.body:
## High-yield amendments

| Amendment | Year | Key change |
|---|---|---|
| **1st** | 1951 | Added **Ninth Schedule**; Articles 31A & 31B (land reform) |
| **7th** | 1956 | Reorganisation of states — 14 states, 6 UTs |
| **42nd** ('Mini-Constitution') | 1976 | **Socialist, Secular, Integrity** in Preamble; **Fundamental Duties** (Part IVA); All-India Judicial Service |
| **44th** | 1978 | Right to property → legal right (**Art 300A**); shields Arts 20 & 21 in emergency |
| **52nd** | 1985 | **Anti-defection law**, Tenth Schedule |
| **61st** | 1989 | Voting age **21 → 18** |
| **73rd & 74th** | 1992 | Panchayats & urban local bodies (Schedules **11 & 12**) |
| **86th** | 2002 | **Right to Education** (Art 21A) |
| **91st** | 2003 | Capped Council of Ministers at 15%; tightened anti-defection |
| **101st** | 2016 | **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** |
| **102nd** | 2018 | Constitutional status to **NCBC** |
| **103rd** | 2019 | **10% EWS** reservation |
| **105th** | 2021 | Restored states' power to identify **SEBCs** |
| **106th** | 2023 | **Women's Reservation** (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) — 1/3 seats |

- The **106th Amendment (2023)** is the **latest** amendment as of 2026.
keyPoints: 1st Amendment (1951) added the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A/31B.
42nd Amendment (1976), the 'Mini-Constitution', added Socialist/Secular/Integrity and Fundamental Duties.
44th Amendment (1978) made the right to property a legal right under Article 300A.
61st Amendment (1989) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.
73rd & 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayats and urban local bodies.
101st (2016) introduced GST; 103rd (2019) gave 10% EWS reservation.
106th Amendment (2023) reserves one-third of seats for women — the latest amendment as of 2026.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Amendments; 106th verified via Wikipedia (2023)

items.title: The Basic Structure Doctrine
items.body:
## Origin

- Laid down in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)** by a **13-judge bench** (largest in Indian history). Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but **cannot destroy or alter its 'basic structure'**.
- The judgment date, **24 April 1973**, became the cut-off used in later cases.

## Elements of the basic structure

- Supremacy of the Constitution
- Republican and democratic form of government
- Secular character; Federalism
- Separation of powers
- **Judicial review** and the rule of law
- Free and fair elections; unity and integrity of the nation

## Reinforcement

- **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down clauses (4) & (5) of Article 368, holding **judicial review** and the FR–DPSP balance to be basic features — 'the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme'.
- **Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** was the **first case to apply the doctrine to strike down a constitutional provision** — the **39th Amendment** clause placing the PM's election beyond judicial review was void for violating **free & fair elections / judicial review**.
- **Waman Rao (1981)** applied the test prospectively — to amendments after 24 April 1973.
- **I.R. Coelho (2007)** held that **Ninth Schedule** laws added after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review.
keyPoints: Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a 13-judge bench, propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine.
Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
Elements include supremacy of the Constitution, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, judicial review and rule of law.
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) first applied the doctrine to strike a constitutional provision — the 39th Amendment clause on the PM's election.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Article 368 (4) & (5) and affirmed judicial review as basic.
I.R. Coelho (2007) made post-24-April-1973 Ninth Schedule laws reviewable.
items.mnemonic: Kesavananda = '13 judges, 1973' — the birth of basic structure.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Important Constitutional Cases

items.title: Amendability of Fundamental Rights — The Case Line
items.body:
## Evolution of precedent

| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Shankari Prasad** | 1951 | Parliament **can** amend Fundamental Rights under Art 368; 'law' in Art 13(2) excludes constitutional amendments |
| **Sajjan Singh** | 1965 | Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad |
| **Golaknath** | 1967 | Parliament **cannot** amend Part III to abridge FRs; an amendment **is** 'law' under Art 13 |
| **Kesavananda Bharati** | 1973 | **Overruled Golaknath**; amendment is not 'law', but subject to the **basic structure** test |
| **Minerva Mills** | 1980 | Judicial review is part of the basic structure |
| **I.R. Coelho** | 2007 | Ninth Schedule laws (post-1973) subject to review |

## Parliament's response

- The **24th Amendment (1971)** was enacted after Golaknath to affirm Parliament's power to amend **any** part, including Fundamental Rights, and to make presidential assent mandatory.
- The net position: Parliament's amending power is **wide but not unlimited** — it is bounded by the basic structure.
keyPoints: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Golaknath (1967) held Fundamental Rights unamendable, treating an amendment as 'law' under Article 13.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golaknath and introduced the basic-structure limit.
The 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part and made assent mandatory.
Parliament's amending power is wide but bounded by the basic structure.
items.mnemonic: Amendability tug-of-war: 'Can (1951) → Cannot (1967) → Can, but not the core (1973)'.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Important Constitutional Cases
